articles.title_orig: Weil Gotshal law firm plans to dissolve, capping dizzying fall
articles.title_zh: Weil Gotshal law firm plans to dissolve, capping dizzying fall
articles.content_orig:
Leaders at Weil, Gotshal & Manges, the nearly century-old law firm that worked for companies from the Lehman Brothers to General Motors, recommended on Wednesday that the firm shut down.
“Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm’s Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down,” a Weil spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.
The firm’s partners are expected to vote on the recommendation “in the coming days,” according to the statement. Equity partners hold stakes in law firms and can vote on company matters.
For over 90 years, the law firm was well-known through Wall Street for steering high-profile corporate litigation such as bankruptcies and mergers. Weil advised the Lehman Brothers during the 2008 financial crisis, and the firm claims it brought General Motors out of bankruptcy in “just 40 days.”
The firm said it guided debtors such as Enron, whose 2001 bankruptcy filing was the largest in American history at the time. It also advised Microsoft’s $68.7 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard as well as AT&T’s acquisition of DirecTV .
The firm had been mired by an exodus of prominent partners, largely driven by competition from rivals, legal news outlet Law.com earlier reported . And a potential merger with another law firm, Willkie Farr, fell through this year.
Weil is announcing its closure without filing for bankruptcy.
The news sent shockwaves through the Big Law industry, which has been going through its own changes. Big mergers and acquisitions have led to more competition for top talent – and then there’s the looming dread of artificial intelligence.
Weil was founded in 1931 and employs approximately 1,200 lawyers in offices from New York to Munich to Hong Kong, according to its website. The firm did not announce plans for its employees or office spaces on Wednesday.

articles.title_zh: Microsoft expects 'very few people' to accept buyout, CFO says in internal memo
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft expects 3,000 or fewer employees to accept the buyout it offered this week to more than a quarter of its workforce, a spokesperson told Business Insider.
The point was reiterated on Wednesday by Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood, who wrote in an internal memo that employees have been questioning the rationale behind the buyout.
"I know there have been some questions on the rationale behind the voluntary exit offer that we announced this week," Hood wrote. "Our intent is to offer employees agency if they choose to leave the company on their own terms. We expect very few people to select this offer because of the growth opportunities here at Microsoft."
The memo statement was part of a quarterly earnings email Hood typically sends internally to employees every quarter when Microsoft discloses its financials.
These memos mostly repeat what the company reports publicly, but this time Hood went out of her way to address the buyout offer, which caused quite a stir across the tech industry this week.
Earlier this year, Microsoft offered a different retirement buyout. In that situation, about one-third of eligible employees took the offer, and that helped Microsoft cut fewer employees in subsequent layoffs.
This week's buyout is getting a lot less uptake, according to the company.
This afternoon, we announced our first-quarter financial results. We exceeded Wall Street expectations, growing revenue 19% and operating income 21%.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
With the start of FY27, we also made an important change to how we report our business. We announced that we changed our reporting structure for the first time in 12 years, moving from three segments to two: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. This change better reflects how we are running the business today — from how we build products and allocate resources to how we create value for customers across the connected layers of our platform. To give you a sense of the two segments, looking back to last fiscal year, Agents and Infra would have represented about 81% of our revenue while Devices and Consumer would have been 19%.
A few highlights from the quarter across our two new segments:
Thank you for everything you did to deliver a strong start to the year. In particular, I want to thank our engineering and capacity delivery teams who are working to help us deliver more capacity faster and with high reliability. These teams are also using the capacity we have more efficiently to create room for us to better meet customer demand for the Azure platform, which continues to exceed our supply.
I know there have been some questions on the rationale behind the voluntary exit offer that we announced this week. Our intent is to offer employees agency if they choose to leave the company on their own terms. We expect very few people to select this offer because of the growth opportunities here at Microsoft. We'll continue to provide a broad set of options for employees to learn, gain new skills, and advance their careers here.
We have tremendous opportunity ahead of us. To meet the moment, we are focused on delivering great products and solutions that help our customers to achieve their many goals — security, innovation, growth — to name a few. Thank you for keeping positive, value-creating outcomes for our customers at the top of the list.
To hear more details about the quarter and our outlook for Q2, you can join live today at 2:30PM Pacific Time, listen on-demand, or read the transcript on the Investor Relations website. articles.title_orig: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.title_zh: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike.
The Fed's benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Here are the key takeaways from the Fed's statement and Fed Chairman Warsh's press conference:
Fed upgrades economy from "solid" to "strong": The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation.
But "inflation remains elevated": Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data.
Warsh announces changes to the Fed's schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy.
Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that "politics played no role in the decision" — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he doesn't agree that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on artificial intelligence, given the strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect.
"I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything."
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post last month on X , expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI.
"What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?"
Warsh pointed to how credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies to invest.
"With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," said Warsh. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.
But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters.
"I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political."
When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt.
"Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets .
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
Wall Street can't make up its mind about the Fed.
Stocks dipped after the 2 p.m. statement, rallied as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke, then gave much of that back. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is holding a small gain, and chip stocks are doing most of the lifting.
The typical stock isn't doing as well. The equal-weighted S&P 500, which gives every company the same weight, is in the red. So are small caps.
The bond market is clearer about what it thinks. The 30-year Treasury yield is near its high of the day, and the 10-year yield is back above 5%. Higher long-term rates make borrowing more expensive for companies and homebuyers.
The dollar moved the other way and slipped against the euro during the press conference.
That leaves the streak. The S&P 500 came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, the second-longest run since 1994, which we pointed out at 2:43 p.m. ET. A higher close would end it, and a lower one would tie the 2018 record of seven.
Chairman Warsh said a couple of words on the Fed's independence amid some discussion that the US midterm elections — just six days away — and the perception that the Fed could influence them could sway the Fed's decision.
"Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
"But I will say," Warsh added, "it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics."
The Fed won't be sitting on its hands for long, says the market.
Traders see about an 85% chance that the Fed raises its benchmark rate by a quarter point at its next meeting on Dec. 9, according to Bloomberg data. The data comes from futures contracts that let traders bet on where the Fed sets rates. Those odds are about where they stood Tuesday, before the decision.
Further out, traders expect the Fed's rate to climb from about 3.9% now to nearly 4.7% by September 2027. That's about three more quarter-point hikes, slightly more than they expected Tuesday.
The Dec. 9 meeting is next. A hike would match what traders already expect. Another hold would mean they've gotten ahead of the Fed.
Chairman Warsh noted that while the Fed waits to assess more inflation data, some policymakers view the central bank's moves so far as beginning to take effect.
"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said.
"If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he added. "What we decided to do was to call these questions, take stock of where we are, evaluate what we're seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol."

articles.title_orig: Dutch Zookeeper Dies After Rare Mauling by a Leopard
articles.title_zh: Dutch Zookeeper Dies After Rare Mauling by a Leopard
articles.content_orig:
A zookeeper has died from her injuries days after she was attacked by a leopard at the Dutch safari park where she worked.
The unnamed employee, who had worked at the Beekse Bergen safari park for almost four decades, was attacked by the animal on Saturday and died on Tuesday.
“With enormous sadness, we have to report that the animal caretaker of safari park Beekse Bergen passed away today from the injuries she sustained on Saturday, October 24, in an incident with a leopard in the park,” the park said in a statement Tuesday.
“Her passing also deeply affects us all, and we are intensely grieving with her family, friends and loved ones. We ask for peace and privacy for her loved ones and our staff, so that they can process this profound loss,” the statement added.
The woman suffered serious wounds to her head and neck while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards, the Associated Press reported.
The woman contacted colleagues via a walkie talkie after the incident in the leopard’s enclosure and an ambulance and trauma helicopter were dispatched at around 11 a.m. local time Saturday, AP added. She underwent emergency surgery but her condition worsened on Sunday evening.
The employee joined the park, located in the southern Netherlands, when she was 17 years old and had worked there “with short breaks for almost 40 years,” the park’s statement added.
CNN affiliate NOS reported that the zookeeper had been working with the leopards for eight years and had been working alone in the enclosure with two male Persian leopards when she was attacked.
There are no cameras inside the enclosure, the park told NOS, which also reported that the animals have been treated as normal since the incident.
The park said that an independent investigation had been launched into the woman’s death.
Rhino kills zookeeper and seriously injures another in Austria
Home to more than 100 species of animals, Beekse Bergen offers visitors the choice of seeing the safari park by foot, car, bus and boat.
This is not the first time a member of staff at a zoo or safari park has been fatally injured by an animal.
In 2023, a zookeeper was killed in Austria after being attacked by a rhino. The incident, in which another zookeeper was injured, occurred at Salzburg Hellbrunn Zoo. Two years prior to that, a woman working at a safari park in Chile was killed by a tiger while working in the big cats’ enclosure.
CNN’s Rose Roobeek contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.title_zh: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.content_orig:
An Iranian flag is seen as missiles and air defense systems are displayed at Baharestan Square in Tehran, Iran, on September 29, 2026.
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao , were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “ finishing the job ” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain , the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned . The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “ smuggling ” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali , an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi , strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi , chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. articles.title_orig: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.title_zh: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.content_orig:
The leader of Israel’s Balad party has condemned the country’s main political leaders for refusing to form a coalition with Arab parties, even after a record showing in polls could make them kingmakers for the next parliament after no clear winner emerged.
Sami Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, are being treated as illegitimate partners despite their turnout.
“This is racism,” he said. “We are a legitimate elected leadership of the national minority. The vast majority of our people decided that we are their leadership.”
Arab parties are on course to win a record 19 seats, giving them potentially decisive leverage over the main political blocs. With 85 percent of the vote counted, Israel’s Central Elections Committee has Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc ahead with at least 53 seats, and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot on 48.
Both are short of the 61 needed to govern. Netanyahu says Israelis chose a strong right-wing government, while Eisenkot says they voted for change.
Abu Shehadeh, who leads Balad, one of the Joint List’s three parties, was not a candidate.
Israel’s elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.
Abu Shehadeh subsequently told the Supreme Court he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
He withdrew in October after a majority of the Supreme Court panel appeared willing to approve the disqualification. He rejects the grounds and said the court had made clear that Israel has “two different judicial systems, one for the Jews and one for the Arabs”.
“We are very proud of the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel that went in this very high percentage of voting,” he told Al Jazeera. The community’s first promise to voters, he said, was to prevent “this gang of criminals” from returning to power, naming Netanyahu and far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. “So our first promise, we can keep it from now .”
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu “has scared off everybody from talking to the Palestinian Israeli parties”, leaving him best placed to “call the shots”. She said that Eisenkot and his allies have indicated that they want a Zionist government and “do not want to form a government” with the Arab parties, leaving them few options.
Danny Ayalon, a former Israeli ambassador to the United States, told Al Jazeera that turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel came in “really unprecedented numbers” and that the parties “are going to have some significant clout”.
Mathematically, he said, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the two Arab parties and pass the threshold, though it would take “political wizardry”. Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List, has said his alliance’s “hands are extended” to oust Netanyahu.
Abu Shehadeh set out what Palestinian citizens want from the next government.
“We are against genocide and we are against apartheid. We want to promote a different political alternative, one which is based on the values of freedom, justice and equality for both people who are living between the river and the sea.”
Of Netanyahu, he said: “Our problem … is that he is a war criminal.”
A UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 for war crimes during the Gaza war.

Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike.
The Fed's benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Here are the key takeaways from the Fed's statement and Fed Chairman Warsh's press conference:
Fed upgrades economy from "solid" to "strong": The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation.
But "inflation remains elevated": Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data.
Warsh announces changes to the Fed's schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy.
Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that "politics played no role in the decision" — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he doesn't agree that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on artificial intelligence, given the strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect.
"I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything."
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post last month on X , expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI.
"What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?"
Warsh pointed to how credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies to invest.
"With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," said Warsh. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.
But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters.
"I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political."
When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt.
"Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets .
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
Wall Street can't make up its mind about the Fed.
Stocks dipped after the 2 p.m. statement, rallied as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke, then gave much of that back. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is holding a small gain, and chip stocks are doing most of the lifting.

The dollar moved the other way and slipped against the euro during the press conference.
That leaves the streak. The S&P 500 came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, the second-longest run since 1994, which we pointed out at 2:43 p.m. ET. A higher close would end it, and a lower one would tie the 2018 record of seven.

"Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
"But I will say," Warsh added, "it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics."

"If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he added. articles.title_zh: Balad leader blasts ‘racist’ exclusion of Arab parties in Israel
articles.content_orig:
A woman carries a child past a sign displaying political parties' electoral symbols at a polling station in the southern Bedouin city of Rahat, Israel, on Oct. 27, during Israel's parliamentary election. Hazem Bader/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The strong showing by Arab-led parties in Israel's election has raised a question for the opposition: Will its leaders work with them to form a government?
Political observers doubt such a partnership will materialize, given the unwillingness of several opposition leaders to work with Arab-led parties. Alon Pinkas, an Israeli political analyst and former diplomat who advised former Prime Ministers Ehud Barak and Shimon Peres, called that reluctance "myopic and reckless."
Pinkas told Morning Edition that opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot could either form a coalition with the parties or establish a minority government with their outside support, allowing them to back major legislation and confidence votes without formally joining the coalition.
But both Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have rejected working with Arab-led parties, which draw much of their support from Palestinian citizens of Israel. Netanyahu went further, calling the prospect of a government relying on their support "a shame and a disgrace."
Speaking with NPR's Steve Inskeep, Pinkas challenged arguments that relying on Arab-led parties would undermine Israel's identity as a Jewish state. He questioned why the same reasoning would not apply to ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, which he said describe themselves as non-Zionist.
Pinkas attributed growing support for Arab-led parties to rising crime and murder rates in Arab communities, particularly violence involving organized crime groups. He said Netanyahu's government had "willfully ignored their plight" by failing to deploy police or investigate the killings.
As for Netanyahu's chances of forming a government, his assessment was emphatic: "Mr. Netanyahu cannot. I repeat, cannot form a government."

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US FTC demands Walmart, Uber, Delta and others hand over data on personalized pricing
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US FTC demands Walmart, Uber, Delta and others hand over data on personalized pricing
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Trade Commission is demanding information from Walmart , Uber and seven other companies on whether and how they use consumers' personal data such as location, browsing history and income to set individual prices, wages and job offers, a senior FTC official told Reuters on Wednesday.
The FTC is flexing its consumer protection powers ahead of the U.S. congressional elections next week, as voters consistently rank the cost of living as the most important issue.
Target , along with app services Lyft , DoorDash and Instacart, and airlines Delta , United , JetBlue , are also receiving demands, the official said.
The FTC will use the information to eventually publish a study to help inform regulators and lawmakers about personalized pricing and wage setting practices.
The advance of algorithmic pricing technology, including tools that incorporate AI, has fueled concern that companies are able to set prices for shoppers on an individual basis in order to extract the maximum price each shopper would be willing to pay.
Personalized pricing strategies are difficult to observe from the outside, because they serve different prices to different people. The FTC study aims to fill in that knowledge gap, demanding comprehensive information about the tools, strategies, and data companies use as well as how they affect prices, wages and job offers.
Efforts by state lawmakers to ban personalized pricing, along with the use of algorithms to individually tailor wages, have taken off in recent years.
The National Retail Federation has criticized the laws and defended retailers' use of data-driven discounts as a means of incentivizing loyalty.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson has said personalizing pricing could violate consumer protection laws where consumers do not expect it and that companies should expect enforcement.
After the FTC called for public comment, hundreds of commenters urged the FTC to ban the practice outright. The FTC has said it does not have the authority to issue a blanket prohibition against the practice.

articles.title_orig: Iran sees only unacceptable ideas in latest mediation to end war, official says
articles.title_zh: Iran sees only unacceptable ideas in latest mediation to end war, official says
articles.content_orig:
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said Wednesday the Iran-backed Lebanese movement was not concerned with the results of Israel's election , vowing to continue its "resistance" against the neighbouring country no matter who wins.
With 85% of ballots counted, the right-wing bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a slight lead over the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, but was still short of a majority after Tuesday's election.
"We do not concern ourselves with who governs Israel, but let it be perfectly clear that it cannot continue its occupation and must leave our land," Qassem said in a written statement.
"The resistance will continue ... and will stand up to the aggression directed against it and against Lebanon, and there is no room to discuss the disarmament" of Hezbollah "as long as the occupation persists and its aggression continues," he added.
The group, which once dominated political life in Lebanon, has been weakened by the two wars it has waged against Israel since 2023.
U.K. Treasury chief John Healey used his first budget Wednesday to offer households and businesses some support with energy bills this winter in the face of what he termed "global economic storms."
He said that his "choice in the budget today is to give families and businesses some breathing space now," as the consequences of the Middle East conflict play out.
"For families, that means higher prices at the pump, higher energy bills and higher mortgages," he said in his statement, one of the main dates of the parliamentary calendar. "For businesses, higher running costs and more expensive loans. And the impact is felt in the public finances, too."
Among the measures announced was a 100-pound ($133) one-off payment this winter for 20 million lower- and middle-income households, proportionately more of whom live in the electoral battlegrounds in northern England.
Other measures include the extension of a cut in the sales tax on electricity bills and the abolition of a charge paid on gas bills.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the Arab parties of stealing the election through widespread fraud and called on Shin Bet, Israel's security agency, to investigate.
"We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals," Netanyahu's Likud party shared on his X account , translated from Hebrew. "This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens. The law enforcement agencies must act with an iron fist and in an immediate manner."
Netanyahu's party leads in the latest vote counts , but all of the parties will fall short of the majority needed to control the Knesset, Israel's parliament. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.
Local media projected 53 seats for the Likud party, 48 seats for the Yahar and other opposition parties and 19 seats for the Arab-led parties. In order to reach a majority (61 of 120 seats) and pick a prime minister, deals will have to be made.
Amid reports Iran had rejected the latest proposal for peace from Qatari intermediaries, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that his country continues to review ideas for a diplomatic solution to the eight-month war.
"While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi wrote. "We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."
The seven-day plan was presented to the U.S. shortly after the U.N. General Assembly in September. However, President Trump rejected the idea presented by Iran for a seven-day ceasefire and then phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
A source had earlier reported there were concerns Israel could begin a new bombing campaign after its election, according to Reuters.
Kuwait summoned Iran's envoy in protest on Wednesday, after Tehran denied one of its citizens, sentenced to death in Kuwait, was involved in an assassination plot targeting a top government figure.
Earlier this week, two Kuwaiti judicial sources told the AFP news agency that the Gulf state had condemned three Shia men to death for plotting the assassination of Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Fahad al-Yousef, collaborating with Iran; and for membership in Hezbollah.
Iran's embassy in Kuwait said earlier Wednesday it "rejects the Kuwaiti government's claim regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate figures or in any other act that could harm Kuwaiti national security."
It added that the person in question had been outside Kuwait for 10 years.
It said it regretted a "negative approach towards Iran, manifested, among other things, in the repetition of flimsy and worn-out scenarios concerning Iranian interference in Kuwaiti affairs."
In response, Kuwait summoned Iranian ambassador Mohammad Toutounji over the statement, which it said "constituted blatant interference in the internal affairs of the State of Kuwait and an infringement upon its sovereignty and the independence of its judiciary."
Abdulredha Haydar Dahqani was among those who had been sentenced to death, the judicial sources told AFP.
Dahqani, an Iranian national, had already been handed the death penalty in 2016 after he was tried in absentia along with 25 Kuwaitis. He was convicted of spying for Iran and plotting attacks.
Another was Hussein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Kuwait's most influential Shia movement, the sources said.
Israel's defense minister on Wednesday denounced opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot for urging the military to resist post-election pressure from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has threatened new strikes on Iran.
"His call to senior military officials not to obey the directives of the prime minister or me or of other relevant security authorities, on the grounds that 'they have his support,' is an anti-democratic statement detached from reality," Israel Katz wrote on X .
Eisenkot, a former military chief, said in a speech to supporters after Tuesday's election that Netanyahu was a caretaker prime minister lacking a mandate and the military should serve the state rather than the premier.
"Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you. You have my unequivocal backing. Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened in recent days to renew strikes on Iran.
Media reports, denied by Netanyahu, said military chief Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir pushed back immediately before the election on the prime minister's new plans on Iran.
Eisenkot's comments were the latest in "a campaign of lies" about tension between Netanyahu and the military over Iran, Katz said.
Yemen's Ministry of Transport has warned of risks to civil aviation safety after Aden International Airport was targeted in a missile attack attributed to the Houthi group for the sixth time, Saudi Arabia's Asharq News reported.
The missile strike shook parts of the southern city, raising fresh concerns over the safety of airport operations and the potential threat to civilian air traffic.
Airport authorities had evacuated all employees and workers from the facility following Houthi threats to target the airport.
Iran is finalizing a protocol with Russia to accelerate joint development of small modular nuclear reactors, Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman and deputy for international, legal and parliamentary affairs at the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, has announced.

articles.title_orig: FedEx beats expectations, raises outlook in first report since calendar adjustment
articles.title_zh: FedEx beats expectations, raises outlook in first report since calendar adjustment
articles.content_orig:
FedEx on Wednesday reported quarterly earnings that beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines and raised its full-year outlook for its newly realigned fiscal year.
Shares of the company fell slightly in extended trading.
Here's how the company performed for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
The company reported net income for the quarter of $290 million, or $1.21 per share, compared with $650 million, or $2.73 per share, during the comparable period a year prior. Adjusting for one-time items — including losses related to short-term investments, gains on the extinguishment of debt and certain restructuring costs — FedEx reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.74.
It marks the first report of FedEx's realigned fiscal year, moving the end of its calendar from May 31 to Dec. 31. The report also comes after the company successfully spun out FedEx Freight into a separate publicly traded company.
FedEx said its express U.S. segment operating income increased in the quarter, primarily driven by higher package yields and volume.
"As our strong operating results and adjusted free cash flow demonstrate, FedEx is winning across high-value market segments while we optimize our network, driving an increase to our full-year outlook," CEO Raj Subramaniam said in a statement.
For the full year, the company is now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $18 and $18.60, compared with a prior range of $16.90 to $18.10. FedEx also said it's revising its 2026 revenue growth expectation to a roughly 12% year-over-year increase, up from previous guidance of an 11% increase.
Earlier this week, FedEx named former AutoZone executive Jamere Jackson as the company's new chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. He replaces Claude Russ, who served as the interim CFO since June 1. John Dietrich was announced as stepping down from that role in April.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Reports Quarterly Cloud Sales That Beat Estimates
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Reports Quarterly Cloud Sales That Beat Estimates
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases."
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Nelson Peltz’s Trian Offers to Buy Wendy’s for $1.4 Billion
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Nelson Peltz’s Trian Offers to Buy Wendy’s for $1.4 Billion
articles.content_orig:
A group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management has offered $1.4 billion to buy Wendy's , according to a regulatory filing Wednesday.
The group has offered $7.35 per share in cash to take the burger chain private, paying a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. In addition to Trian, it includes investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
Wendy's shares spiked about 15% in morning trading following the offer. The Wall Street Journal first reported Peltz's proposal.
Wendy's did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Trian declined to comment beyond the filing.
The take-private deal offer comes after a tough two-year stretch for the burger chain. Wendy's stock has tumbled 65% over that period, including Wednesday's gains. For six straight quarters, the company has reported same-store sales declines.
Wendy's is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings before the bell on Nov. 5.
Wendy's challenges have made the company a cheaper acquisition target for Peltz, whose history with the brand dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago.
Budget-conscious diners have been eating out less often, and Wendy's and its rivals have leaned into discounts to lure consumers into restaurants. Wendy's has also dealt with a revolving door of chief executives, who have had different ideas about turnaround strategies for the struggling chain.
"In our view, a take private makes sense as Wendy's turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category," TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday.
In May, former Potbelly CEO Bob Wright joined Wendy's as its latest chief executive, after his former employer went private. In his first earnings conference call with analysts in August, he was candid about what he views as the chain's biggest issues, like muddled value offerings, inconsistent execution at its restaurants and too many one-off promotions.
Trian previously explored a takeover of Wendy's in 2022, but later decided against it. The firm and affiliated parties own a 16.25% stake in Wendy's, according to the regulatory filing, making them the company's largest shareholder.

articles.title_orig: Perv teacher learns fate for sex with 2 students — that already ended her job and marriage
articles.title_zh: Perv teacher learns fate for sex with 2 students — that already ended her job and marriage
articles.content_orig:
A married teacher in Australia was on Wednesday sentenced to just over a year in jail for having sex with two teenage students — which she tried to blame on “irresistible” impulses driven by bipolar disorder.
Tayla Lee Brailey , 32, wept as she hugged her parents and several supporters at her sentencing in Sydney on Wednesday — after already having lost her job and her husband after admitting her twisted crimes, Australian outlet ABC reported .
Brailey was first arrested in August 2024 for having sex with a 17-year-old boy in her car, returning to her classes after the sordid hookup.
She was released on bail — just to be busted again a few weeks later when it emerged she’d also touched a 16-year-old student’s genitals in her classroom, an experience that he said in a victim statement still overwhelms him with shame.
Brailey had groomed that younger victim online, according to the Canberra Times , sending him a naked picture of her in the shower and asking, “Do you like what you see?”
She then made him send her a nude in return. “Yum,” she replied to the 16-year-old student. “Stay back with me after school,” she wrote — with them kissing and touching each other’s genitals in her classroom.
“He has been feeling ashamed and had to leave high school before he finished … because of the shame he felt,” the judge, Justice Elizabeth Ryan, said during Bailey’s sentencing.
“He had suffered lack of sleep and flashbacks … he said none of his friends at high school speak to him anymore.”
The judge was told that Brailey was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder, creating impaired judgment and increased sex drive, leaving her with an “irresistible impulse” for sex with the boys, as the Australian also reported.
The judge, however, said that while Brailey’s crimes may have been “terrible mistakes,” she “used her position as a teacher … to abuse the trust of two young persons.”
“It is also relevant that she knew what she was doing was wrong but persisted with it,” Judge Ryan said.
“Offences like this cause immense harm to the trust that must exist between families and the education system,” the judge said.
“For these reasons … no penalty other than imprisonment is appropriate.”
Brailey was sentenced to nine months in prison for having sex with the 17-year-old student, and a year for sexually touching the 16-year-old boy, with an aggregate term of 15 months in jail.
She will also be placed on the child protection register for 15 years.
The teacher — who has since trained as an accountant — will be eligible for parole in April 2027.

Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.
The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.
This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.
“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.
The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies , which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.
In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.
“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.
“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.
The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.
The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.
Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.
Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.
However, the term “ associate member ” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.
“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.
“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.
“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.
Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.
He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.
Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.
“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.
Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

articles.title_orig: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.title_zh: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.content_orig:
At least 68 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, authorities have said.
The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. It occurred on the Madrid to Seville line.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the control system at the nearby town of Urda failed and six trains were stopped. One was allowed to restart and travelled 25km before hitting a stopped train at high speed, he added, saying it was "inexplicable" how this had happened.
As well as those killed, 50 people were also injured, the minister said.
Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported .
The local Castilla-La Mancha government confirmed at least 68 people had died, higher than another high-speed crash in southern Spain that killed 45 people in January.
Emiliano García-Page, the president of the region, said 24 people had died on a train operated by rail company Renfe, with the rest killed on a train operated by Iryo.
More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, newspaper El País said.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by the Renfe train, saying the cause was "still unknown".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a post on X that he was "shocked" by the accident.
"If there has been any negligence, it will come to light," he later said at a press conference.
"If there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness. It is clear that we have experienced two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail within the same year."
Sanchez's political future will be tested in a snap election on Nov. 29, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis.
Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday.
"Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in a post on X.
— CNBC's Charlotte Reed contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Fed meeting recap: Warsh says central bank will host fewer rate-setting meetings in future years
articles.title_zh: Fed meeting recap: Warsh says central bank will host fewer rate-setting meetings in future years
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady . At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead.
Here are five key takeaways:
"The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management.
"The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. We expect a hike in December and another in early 2027." — Seema Shah, chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management .
"We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies .

articles.title_orig: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
articles.title_zh: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has emerged as the critical sticking point between the U.S. and China. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition.
Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms.
Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI.
“We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said.
During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said.
Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology.
At the summit, the U.S. and China agreed to extend a trade truce until January. No agreement was reached on implementing safeguards for AI.
Trump and Xi are set to meet again in China next month.

articles.title_orig: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state’s total ban on gambling
articles.title_zh: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state’s total ban on gambling
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.
Utah, which prohibits gambling, sued Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.
“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).
The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said yesterday . “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.”
If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products , including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC.
The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filed lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases.
“Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.”
The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with by courts throughout the US are whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws.
The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor. Kalshi sued Utah in February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market.
In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelby wrote , “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.”
Shelby determined the text of US law makes it clear that state regulation is not forbidden. US law states that CFTC jurisdiction does not “supersede or limit the jurisdiction conferred on courts of the United States or any State,” and “explicitly provides for State regulation of its gaming laws in all but a few specified cases,” he wrote.
“Congress is aware that some States permit gambling while others do not, and the CEA explicitly provides for State jurisdiction,” Shelby wrote.
Kalshi is now appealing its loss to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit but was unable to obtain an injunction preventing enforcement of the state gambling ban while that litigation continues. On September 8, Tenth Circuit judges denied Kalshi’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal. Utah filed its lawsuit seeking a shutdown of Kalshi about six weeks later.
The CFTC lawsuit against Utah makes arguments similar to the ones already rejected by the district court, although some other courts have ruled otherwise.
“Utah is not the first State that has attempted to invade the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over swaps,” the CFTC lawsuit said. “Already, several federal courts—including the Third Circuit—have swiftly responded by issuing or affirming temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions barring the States from enforcing their gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges that offer sports-related or other event contracts.”
The Third Circuit appeals court ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. But Kalshi lost similar cases in the Sixth Circuit and Ninth Circuit in rulings that went in favor of Ohio, Tennessee, and Nevada.
Because circuit appeals courts are divided on the issue, it is likely that the Supreme Court will take up the case and determine whether states can apply their gambling laws to prediction markets. New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Court to resolve the circuit split, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s petition.

articles.content_orig:

Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents.
The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.
Apeiron was one of four finalist names that Virgin Galactic narrowed down from a list of 276 employee-submitted suggestions. After the public weighed in, Apeiron came out on top over Horizon, Explorer and Ascend.
“Apeiron, the Boundless, captures the ambition of human spaceflight and the possibilities it opens for humanity," Virgin Galactic CEO Michael Golglazier said in a company statement. "The extraordinary response to the public vote made choosing this name even more meaningful."
The shiny new space plane will be attached to Virgin Galactic's VMS Eve carrier aircraft for its journey to Spaceport America, where engineers will complete work on its avionics software ahead of Apeiron's first flight tests and eventual operational missions.
The new Delta-class vehicle replaces Virgin's earlier space plane model, VSS Unity , which flew seven suborbital missions during its operational lifetime between the summers of 2023 and 2024. The company suspended VSS Unity flights to focus efforts on Apeiron's development, and now hopes to begin flying customers again in mid-2027.
Once they're in regular operation, Virgin plans to fly each of its Delta-class vehicles as many as eight times a month. A second Delta-class space plane is already under construction and is expected to join Apeiron at Spaceport America around the same time that Virgin restarts flying passengers, about 675 of whom are still waiting in line with tickets for a seat on one of the company's suborbital jaunts, according to the company's Q2 2026 SEC filing .
Now, more than 100 of those future space travelers are beginning their initial preparations for flight, with more ticketholders expected to follow once Virgin brings the second Delta-class vehicle into service. When the company began selling seats aboard its space plane in 2014, when VSS Unity was still under construction, tickets were priced around $200,000. Today, that price has jumped to $850,000 per seat, according to a report by Latte .
Like its predecessor, Apeiron and future Delta-class vehicles are designed for short, suborbital spaceflights, and are not capable of reaching orbit around Earth . They fly above the internationally recognized boundary of space , the 100-kilometer-high (62 miles) Karman line , and provide those onboard with several minutes of weightlessness and great views of the planet below.
Virgin Galactic plans to share further details about its upcoming flight tests during its November earnings call.
Virgin is one of two American companies that have flown paying customers to suborbital space and back. The other, Blue Origin , suspended its flights earlier this year to focus on helping land NASA astronauts on the moon .
Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram , and follow him on X , where he mostly posts in haiku.
